Our results show that the velocity Verlet algorithm yields the highest precision, while the generalised Verlet algorithm exhibits the best energy conservation. Furthermore, we observe that the optimal time step for the numerical integration is influenced by the choice of FF and electron correlation treatment. Additionally, we find that the energy conservation and precision of the numerical method are directly correlated with the conformational properties of the system. Our findings highlight the importance of selecting an appropriate numerical scheme, in conjunction with an accurate FF, to ensure precise classical atomic dynamics in biomolecular systems. Our data also suggests that, despite minor inaccuracies in energy conservation, the Symplectic Euler method demonstrates comparable precision to the other investigated schemes. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive framework for optimizing numerical methods in classical atomic dynamics simulations of biomolecular systems. The accurate determination of proton distribution functions, particularly at low momentum scales, relies on the closure approximation or numerical solutions of the DGLAP evolution equations. In this work, we bypass these constraints and directly fit PDFs at various scales, using a large set of 2-10 loop approximations of the splitting functions. We achieve this by introducing a linear basis that captures the essential features of the splitting functions and their integrals. This approach allows for the fitting of PDFs at both low and high scales, even in regions close to the endpoint, without the need for closure approximation. We present initial fits to available deep-inelastic scattering data from HERA, fixed target experiments, and some results from early running LHC experiments. We also discuss the importance of resolving the $x$-dependence of PDFs, particularly at the small-$x$ limit, and the implications of our findings on the formation of $\xi$-space PDFs. Additionally, we provide an overview of the proposed fitting protocol in the context of a global PDF analysis.

A bipartite graph is planarizable if it can be drawn in a 2-dimensional plane with no edge intersections. A method called vertex splitting has been proposed to make non-planarizable bipartite graphs planarizable. This technique involves breaking a vertex into multiple subvertices, which are then reconnected through modified edges. A recursive application of this process can transform any bipartite graph into a simpler form called "normal" status, at which point a planar drawing is possible. The exact geometric constraints required for a graph to reach a normal state through vertex splitting have been defined in a previous study. Based on these constraints, precise conditions have been derived to determine in advance whether a given bipartite graph will result in a compact drawing through vertex splitting, without the need for time-consuming optimization. These conditions take the form of linear programs, which can be solved efficiently in a matter of seconds for small to medium-sized graphs. An implementation of these conditions has been integrated into a popular graph drawing software package called Geompack. An extensive evaluation of these conditions has been conducted using a public database of bipartite graphs, which showed significant improvements over existing methods in terms of drawing quality and efficiency. The results achieved with the linear program-based approach have been compared to those obtained through optimization using a different method called Constrained Conformal Quadrangulation, which is known to be more accurate but much more cumbersome to use. The most extensive drawing found in the study consisted of over 10,000 nodes and 20,000 edges, which was achieved through the use of Constrained Conformal Quadrangulation, while the linear program-based approach became too slow for graphs larger than 5,000 nodes. All source code and additional information required to replicate the study has been made available for download. In this model, we explore the concept of contextual learning, where an agent's task context provides additional information that can aid in decision-making. The conventional Sagnac interferometer's sensitivity limitations when detecting gravitational waves in the low-frequency range have led to innovative designs, with the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer being one of the proposed solutions. By introducing fluid dynamics into the interferometer's optical cavity, this design aims to enhance sensitivity by converting gravitational wave-induced cavity length changes into a combination of optical phase shifts and fluid sloshing. As a result, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer can detect weaker phase changes and achieve higher sensitivity, specifically in the 10^-9 radian strain range, which is theoretically possible with an optimal fluid parameter. Furthermore, by scaling the interferometer to a 10 km mirror distance, it is possible to detect a 10^-22 erg/cm^2 signal strength of gravitational wave energy, opening up the potential for detecting gravitational waves of very low frequency, specifically in the 10^-6 Hz range. Additionally, this technology presents an intriguing possibility of detecting dark matter halos through their gravitational field. To physically demonstrate the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's enhanced sensitivity, a simple analogy is provided using a classic mass-spring system, along with a comment on its applicability to superconducting gravitational wave detectors. Moreover, the paper investigates the effects of noise sources, specifically laser noise, thermal noise, and fluid viscosity, to determine the optimal operating parameters for the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer. With an assumed 10 km mirror distance, the results show that increasing the fluid mass can lead to improved sensitivity, but only up to a point, beyond which further growth will result in decreased sensitivity due to increased viscosity-induced noise. Consequently, there is an optimal fluid parameter that maximizes sensitivity, with the 10 km scaled sloshing-Sagnac interferometer achieving the best results with a 20 kg fluid mass, resulting in an improvement of nearly two orders of magnitude over the conventional Sagnac interferometer in terms of minimum detectable strain. Lastly, the paper discusses the feasibility of utilizing existing infrastructure, such as a suspended tunneling electron system, as the fluid mass in the sloshing-Sagnah interferometer, along with the potential for further optimization by introducing multiple fluid layers.

The introduction of neural language models has significantly improved performance in machine translation and summarization, but they are often cumbersome to deploy on limited resources due to their size. In contrast, $N$-gram models are smaller and more portable, which is why we propose combining the two for better results. Specifically, we use a neural language model as a prior distribution for the neural maximum a posteriori estimation of the $N$-gram model, thereby accounting for the fundamental difference in model structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this combination, which we call the neural-assisted $N$-gram model, in three translation tasks and two summarization tasks, achieving notable improvements over both individual models and serving as a strong foundation for neural neural language model classification. Furthermore, we investigate the theoretical properties of the neural-assisted $N$-gram model, including the boundary conditions for the smoothing algorithm and the relationship to the joint maximum a posteriori estimation, which provides valuable insights into the model's behavior. The code is available at https://github.com/MiuLiu1995/Neural-Assisted-Ngram.

The integration of optical character recognition (OCR) systems and mobile phones for vote tabulation faces challenges, primarily due to OCR's error-prone output. We aim to enhance the accuracy of OCR through real-time spell checking on phones, utilizing a large English dictionary. This paper introduces an innovative spell correction approach, leveraging a spell checker and a context that is not too complex for optimal results. We evaluate this algorithm on various text categories and conduct vote tabulation system experiments with real data. The results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness, with average correction rates exceeding 90% for common OCR errors and significant reductions in error frequencies in vote tabulation. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of spell checker dictionary size on algorithm performance and discuss potential limitations. The findings suggest that a spell correction system can significantly enhance OCR accuracy in vote tabulation, with the best model achieving an error rate of 3.5% on a benchmark dataset. This technology holds promise for improving the reliability of OCR-based phone applications in various domains, including language translation and accessibility services for individuals with disabilities. By creating an Earth-like atmosphere on Mars, we identify similar patterns of storm development and the role of temperature gradients in driving these storms. Furthermore, we observe analogous behavior between the Martian storm system and the Earth's stratospheric circulation, with both exhibiting a strong polar jet stream and a weak equatorial jet. These findings suggest that the atmospheres of Earth and an Earth-like Mars would exhibit comparable behavior in terms of storm patterns and circulation systems. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the detection of storm patterns in real Martian data. Lastly, we discuss the potential for future studies to investigate the relationship between storm patterns and the molecular composition of an Earth-like Martian atmosphere. Moreover, we outline the possibilities for using similar atmospheric dynamics as a basis for designing an Earth-like atmosphere on a hypothetical exoplanet.

When comparing the results of these methods, along with standard methods like the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equation and the quantum hydrodynamic model, to data from a established many-body approach, we found that the standard methods often fall short, especially when measuring non-equilibrium effects. On the other hand, the linearized hydrodynamic approach with a stochastic component consistently produced accurate results, even in scenarios with strong non-equilibrium effects, making it an efficient tool for simulating large non-equilibrium quantum systems. Additionally, due to its computational efficiency, we were able to use this approach to calculate the behavior of a massive Reflected Shock Wave in a harmonic cone cavity, which is an intriguing phenomenon that other methods struggle to model. Furthermore, by analyzing the performance of the approach in various situations, we validated its reliability, including situations with rapidly changing conditions, sharp quantum fluctuations, and strong non-equilibrium effects. Moreover, we observed that the approach's accuracy is not compromised by using an ideal gas model, despite the fact that it should be suboptimal for describing condensate collapse and formation, as well as the resulting non-linear effects. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on the minimum energy required for a solitary wave to form in the system. Through a direct approach, we also investigate the stability of solitary waves by linearizing the anharmonic oscillator model around a reference wave and analyzing the spectrum of the resulting linearized operator. This approach enables us to determine the point at which a solitary wave becomes unstable as we vary the parameter gamma. Lastly, we compare the critical values of gamma derived from the stability threshold and the linearized operator spectrum analysis, observing that they coincide when the mass parameter m is less than 1/2. Moreover, we observe that for m > 1/2, the N-body system's behavior differs significantly from that of the single-particle anharmonic oscillator model, with the N-body system's energy growing polynomially rather than exponentially as the distance between the solitary wave and a polaron increases. To identify a neutral long-lived (NLN) particle, we propose a novel detection method that utilizes the extended volume of destruction left behind as it decays. This method is particularly effective in the context of hadron colliders, as it allows for the detection of a particle even as it transitions from the relativistic to the non-relativistic regime. As a result of this detection capability, the search parameters for NLN particles, specifically the decay length threshold, can be optimized. Using a simplified model of a first-generation supersymmetric scenario, we predict that by utilizing this new detection potential, we can discover a majorana neutral lepton that is 10 times more stable than previously possible. Furthermore, historical data from the LHC and future discovery potential at the HL-LHC and a 27 TeV collider are all evaluated to determine their capacity to detect such a particle. Moreover, we explore the production mechanisms by which these long-lived particles would come to exist, and the characteristics of the accompanying jet activity that detectives can utilize to verify their findings. By analyzing the decay patterns of these particles, we determine that their non-relativistic, weak interactions with surrounding matter will either repair themselves or result in the creation of long-lived jets of energy. Consequently, we outline the search strategies that detectors should employ to identify these particles, which include using missing transverse momentum to detect jets that have escaped detection, as well as utilizing the strong interactions that these particles engage in to identify long-lived, weakly interacting particles that have decayed. Additionally, we provide a framework for calculating the cross-sectional area of the process by which a hadron collider discovers a neutral long-lived particle that transitions from the relativistic to the non-relativistic regime, decays, and leaves behind a trail of destruction. Using this framework, we derive the relationship between the production rate of these particles and the characteristics of the neutral long-lived particle itself, which includes its mass, stability, charge, spin, decay constant, and weak coupling strength. Lastly, we analyze the discovery potential of a future 100 TeV collider for a scenario in which a neutral long-lived particle that is similar in nature to an electron comes to exist due to new physics beyond the standard model.

The paper investigates the phenomenon where words with similar meanings in controlled experiments exhibit significant shifts in context, resulting in disparate semantic representations. While previous studies have established this pattern, the paper takes a distinct viewpoint, arguing that the notable changes often observed are not necessarily indicative of actual semantic change. Instead, the authors contend that the context's variability plays a more substantial role in shaping the output, as it does with other language models. A key aspect of a tree action by a group $G$, prior to its classification, is the way it partitions the tree into cells (or cosets of an edge) and the resulting graph of intersections. Especially intriguing is the case of an action by a right-angled Artin group $A_\Delta$, which is defined by a graph $\Delta$ and acts on a tree if and only if $\Delta$ contains no triangles. Moreover, the graph of intersections is a linear tree, and the action is free if and only if $\Delta$ has no cycles of length two. If an action by $A_\Delta$ on a tree $T$ results in a graph of intersections $\Omega$, then it acts on the tree derived from concatenating paths in $\Omega$ in the same way it acts on $T$. This leads to a recursive construction that yields a detailed understanding of the structure of trees of which $A_\Delta$ acts through an action on a tree of cells. This paper explores the scenario where a separating subgraph in the graph of intersections corresponds to a subtree of the tree of which $A_\Delta$ acts, which yields additional information about the structure of the tree of which $A_\Delta$ acts. A key role is played by the following three results: If a graph $\Delta$ contains no cycles of length two or three, then a right-angled Artin group $A_\Delta$ acts on a tree of cells $T$ such that a subgraph in the graph of intersections corresponds to a specific subtree of $T$. Conversely, if a tree of which $A_\Delta$ acts through an action on a tree of cells $T$ contains a subtree that corresponds to a separating subgraph in the graph of intersections, then the subgraph contains no cycles of length two or three. If a graph $\Delta$ contains no cycles of length two, then a right-angled Artin group $A_\Delta$ acts on a tree of cells $T$ such that a subgraph in the graph of intersections corresponds to a specific subtree of $T$, and the structure of $T$ is fully determined by the structures of $\Delta$ and the subgraph. A systematic approach is also presented to construct all trees of which $A_\Delta$ acts through an action on a tree of cells when the graph $\Delta$ contains no cycles of length two, which serves as a classification. This classification is particularly useful for the computation of the number of distinct actions by right-angled Artin groups

In contextual linear bandits, the agent must select actions that maximize rewards in environments defined by a context. A recent study introduced a Regret Minimizing (RM) algorithm that learns the underlying linear reward and context distributions with probability at least $1-\delta$ within a specified error bound. Building upon this research, we developed an adaptive learning strategy called Context-Aware Linear Bandit (CALB) that utilizes a fixed amount of information to precisely define the distribution of the context through a confidence interval. In a recent study, we explored the connection between the CALB algorithm and the underlying linear context distribution, revealing that a significant portion of the information (approximately $n\cdot d$ bits) is required to define the distribution of the context. In a contextual linear bandit setting, we introduced a new algorithm called Compressed Context-Aware Linear Bandit (CCALB) that leverages the established connections between the context, linear reward, and distribution of the context. The CCALB algorithm allows the agent to use a compressed representation of the context to obtain a nearly optimal action, with an average reward approaching the optimal level as the number of actions taken grows. Under the assumption of a finite context distribution with $m$ possible scenarios, the algorithm achieves a time-averaged regret of $O(\sqrt{T \log d / \Delta_{min}})$ within a horizon of $T$ time steps, where $\Delta_{min}$ represents the smallest difference between distinct distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we explored the information required to define the context distribution, revealing that a context distribution with a continuous underlying structure can be precisely defined using an information amount of $n\cdot d$ bits. However, for a discrete distribution with $m$ possible scenarios, we demonstrated that an information amount of $O(n \cdot \log m)$ bits is sufficient to define the distribution, which is more accurate than the previously established bound of $n\cdot d$ bits. Additionally, we explored the relationship between information amount and the achievable average reward, disclosing that an average reward approaching the optimal level is achievable as the number of actions taken grows, even in a setting with a continuous underlying structure of the context distribution. A comparison with existing research on linear bandits revealed that our findings improve upon previously established bounds by an order of magnitude for a discrete distribution with $m$ possible scenarios, with an improvement of m! times for a distribution with a structured underlying structure. This study examines how dust growth influences the cooling behavior in the outer parts of protoplanetary disk systems. A sophisticated model that considers grain growth and settlement, as well as millimeter waves and optical/infrared observations, has been employed to analyze data from the HL Tau and BHB07 systems. To accurately represent the conditions in these systems, we utilized a two-component structure, with a heated inner layer and a cooler outer layer. By analyzing specific vibration peaks of water ice, we determined particle sizes in the HL Tau system to be around 1 millimeter in the outer layer and 10 microns in the inner layer. Furthermore, we observed a decline in dust temperature with decreasing grain growth, which contradicts the expected increase in temperature. This anomaly is attributed to reduced acoustic waves in the outer layer, impeding heat transfer and allowing dust to cool more efficiently. In the case of the BHB07 system, we detected a larger ice settlement depth and larger particle sizes, likely resulting from stronger acoustic waves and increased dust settling. These larger particles obstruct sunlight from reaching inner ice layers, preventing them from thawing and freezing again, which in turn hampers the formation of ring structures in this system. Our findings suggest that dust settling is a crucial factor in creating ring patterns in protoplanetary disk systems and that the presence of rings is not necessarily indicative of active ice layer turbulence. Moreover, we propose that the absence of visible ring structures in many T Tauri stars might be attributed to similar settling-induced silencing of acoustic waves, rather than a lack of ice layers or insufficient mass. Ultimately, our research indicates that dust properties, influenced by settling and growth, play a more significant role in shaping the patterns we observe in protoplanetary disk systems than other considered factors, including magnetic fields and gas properties. Additionally, we observed a positive correlation between dust settling depth and particle sizes in these systems. The model employed in this study also revealed a disconnect between dust and gas temperatures in the outer layer, which could be misinterpreted as evidence of gas evaporation in other analyses. However, our findings confirm that this phenomenon is simply a result of reduced acoustic waves allowing dust to cool more efficiently. This cooling disparity might be observable in the near-infrared and millimeter wave spectra of similar protoplanetary disk systems in the future.

Neural network systems have been compromised by static backdoor attacks, which alter the output of these systems by manipulating input data. In response, researchers have explored the concept of dynamic backdoor attacks that modify input data to inject a backdoor, aiming to disrupt such compromised systems. Despite the development of dynamic backdoor techniques for various classification tasks, primarily in single-task scenarios, we identify a significant gap in the existing literature. Specifically, there is a lack of dynamic backdoor methods that can successfully inject a backdoor in multi-task neural networks. To bridge this gap, we present a dynamic backdoor injection scheme, which we call Adaptive Triggering Pattern Injection, incorporating a neural network to deliver triggering patterns to compromised neural networks. We further introduce a regularized neural network training process to ensure the scheme's effectiveness. Through comprehensive experiments on fake news detection and sentiment analysis, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, achieving accuracy in both healthy and compromised neural network segments. Moreover, we explore the applicability of our ATPI scheme to existing deep learning frameworks and implement it using PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Keras. The code is available for public access. In a single-task scenario, our ATPI approach matches the performance of static backdoor attacks, while outperforming existing dynamic backdoor techniques in terms of success rates. Additionally, we observe that our method can withstand code obfuscation, demonstrating its robustness. In a multi-task scenario, our ATPI scheme surpasses existing dynamic backdoor techniques in success rates and achieves comparable performance to static backdoor attacks. With its high success rate and flexibility, our ATPI scheme offers a strong foundation for future research on dynamic backdoor attacks. The findings presented in this paper can be applied to various neural network systems, enabling the creation of backdoor-embedded models that can be trained using existing deep learning platforms, including Google Colab, Baidu AI Studio, and FATE. The discovery of a hardware-based side-channel vulnerability in neural network systems, which can be exploited to inject a backdoor by modifying triggering pattern delivery, also provides valuable insights. With the development of a hardware-based side-channel attack tool, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our ATPI scheme in defending against such attacks. The research presented in this paper makes a significant contribution to the field of backdoor attacks in neural network systems, offering a dynamic backdoor injection technique that can be employed in various classification tasks, as well as a fundamental understanding of the underlying mechanisms, which will prove beneficial in developing robust detection methods for future work. We demonstrate this by constructing, from single photons, three Gaussian bosonic systems in a specific non-classical state called a "loop state." By showing that entanglement between subsystems is solely responsible for three-way entanglement and steering, we prove that a similar arrangement of an infinite-dimensional harmonic oscillator can exhibit non-locality and steering even among an infinite number of sub-systems. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between one-way classical communication, the "squeezing" parameter, and the measurable reduction in a subsystem's variance upon system steering. Moreover, we identify a minimum non-local connection required between two sub-systems for steering to occur between their counterparts. Lastly, we outline the practical generation of loop states and the implications of our findings for the application of system steering in quantum teleportation and cavity-mediated non-linear interactions.

A key challenge in the development of Hardware Accelerators for Big Data Processing is enhancing throughput while minimizing energy consumption. To address this, our proposed Framework called a Partial Decomposed Hierarchical Tensor (FDHT) is combined with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network model, resulting in what is dubbed an FDHT-LSTM Architecture. By improving upon existing HTM structures such as CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP), our FDHT with a 9th order outperforms in terms of throughput and efficiency, achieving a throughput of 268.3 kilopixels per second and an energy efficiency of 0.032 pixels per Joule. Furthermore, our FDHT with a 3rd order tensor shows comparable performance to a state-of-the-art general-purpose accelerator for an LSTM model, demonstrating its effectiveness. Additionally, our FDHT-LSTM Architecture outperforms conventional HM structures composed of Memory Arrays and Digital Logic in terms of throughput and energy efficiency, achieving a throughput of 12.4 gigapixels per second and an energy efficiency of 0.006 pixels per Joule for a 3rd order tensor. Moreover, our FDHT-LSTM Architecture surpasses a state-of-the-art special-purpose hardware accelerator for an LSTM model in terms of throughput and energy efficiency, demonstrating its practicality. Lastly, by integrating our FDHT-LSTM Architecture with a established RISC-V Processor, we achieve a throughput of 1.3 gigamatrix multiplications per second and an energy efficiency of 0.07 matrix multiplications per Joule for a 3rd order tensor, along with a throughput of 12.7 gigapixels per second and an energy efficiency of 0.006 pixels per Joule for an LSTM model, thereby meeting the needs for high-performance and low-energy Big Data Processing. A figure of merit called an Area-throughput Product (ATP) is also improved upon in our research, achieving an ATP of 682.8 milliom square millimeters for a 3rd order tensor and an ATP of 24.9 million square millimeters for an LSTM model. A prototype of our FDHT-LSTM Architecture is further designed, demonstrating its feasibility. A new perspective is also offered on the relationship between a block size and a memory array's capacity, showing that a larger block size results in a significantly increased capacity.
